title: Grief
hook: Jesus wept; grief is love continuing

segments.voice: Yesterday, when faith and depression meet: Elijah under the juniper tree, and an angel saying arise and eat. Your line was seek help, it's holy. Did you send that message? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

"Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Martha says it on the road outside Bethany, the moment Jesus arrives. Her brother Lazarus has been in the tomb for days. A little later her sister Mary comes out of the house, falls at his feet, and says the very same words. Two sisters, one sentence. If only you had been here. Grieving people still say some version of it, to God, to a doctor, to themselves. And in John's telling, Jesus doesn't correct either of them. Today: grief.

Start with the sentence. If thou hadst been here. It's half complaint and half trust: you could have stopped this, and you didn't come. John lets both sisters say it out loud, and nobody scolds them. Martha keeps talking, and the two of them have a conversation on the road about death and rising again. Grief, in this chapter, is allowed to speak. Next, look at the crowd. A little later come the two words that make up a whole verse in the King James Bible: Jesus wept. And when the mourners see it, they say, "Behold how he loved him!" Not how weak he is. Not how little faith he has. How he loved him. Some do ask why he couldn't have prevented the death, but the first thing John records is love. The tears are read as love made visible. That's the heart of today's line: grief is love continuing after the person is gone. Third, what Paul does and doesn't say. Writing to grieving Christians in Thessalonica, he says he wants them to "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." Notice he doesn't tell them not to sorrow. He talks about how they sorrow: with hope alongside. Some Christians hear that as comfort; some hear it, on hard days, as a weight. Both are honest. Last, the blessing. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." Mourning isn't a problem to be fixed before blessing can arrive. The mourners are the ones named as blessed. Churches carry this in different ways: funerals and wakes, Orthodox memorial services with candles and a sweet dish of wheat, Catholics praying for the dead by name, Protestant families gathering for a meal after the burial. Different customs, one shared instinct: grief is love, and it deserves room.

Here's the practice: let yourself grieve. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone or something you've lost. A person, a friendship, a place, a version of your life. Let one specific memory come: their voice, a kitchen, a phrase they used. Don't hurry it away. If tears come, let them. If nothing comes, that's all right too. If you pray, you can tell God their name. If you don't, just hold the memory a little longer than you usually let yourself. The bell holds the time.
Grief. The sorrow of loss, which Jesus himself wept, and which the crowd at Lazarus's tomb read as love.
Your line: grief is love. Today, say the name of someone you've lost out loud to someone else, and tell them one thing you loved. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Christians mourn through funerals, wakes and shared meals; Catholics pray and offer Masses for the dead, Orthodox Christians hold memorial services, and churches name the dead in prayer, holding sorrow and the hope of resurrection together.

match.prompt: at the tomb of Lazarus — tap the pairs.
pairs: sorrow not, as those with no hope

myth: Martha and Mary each say to Jesus, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died
both sisters say the very same sentence, and he doesn't correct either one.
Paul told grieving Christians not to sorrow at all
he said not to sorrow as others which have no hope: sorrow, with hope alongside.
the mourners read Jesus's tears as love
they said, behold how he loved him, though some also asked why he hadn't prevented the death.

fork.setup: you're Martha. your brother has been in the tomb for days, and Jesus has only now arrived. what do you do?
options: stay in the house and say nothing.
go out to meet him and say it: if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
greet him politely and hide how you feel.
fork.reveal: Martha goes out on the road and says it plainly, and later Mary says the same words. neither is scolded. grief is allowed to speak.

original.note: Greek: he wept, shed tears. John 11:35 reads ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, Jesus wept.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you have faith, you shouldn't grieve.
what it means: both sisters said if only you had been here, nobody scolded them, and when Jesus wept the crowd saw love in it.
what a scholar hears: John uses a quiet word for shedding tears for Jesus, edakrusen, and a louder word for the wailing of Mary and the mourners. his grief is quiet, and real.

notes: Hook avoids calling John 11:35 'the shortest verse' under the claims rule; it says only that the verse is two words in the KJV.
'Lazarus has been in the tomb for days': John 11:17 says four days; kept vague deliberately.
Trapdoor contrasts edakrusen (Jesus, 11:35) with klaiō (Mary and the mourners, 11:33): a lexical claim. Confirm.
Orthodox memorial services with 'a sweet dish of wheat' (koliva): confirm description.
'Grief is love with nowhere to go' is a modern saying, not attributed to any source; used as the lesson's own phrasing. Confirm it reads as such.

Editor pass: day 1380 (A God who suffers) already opened on 'Jesus wept', its two-word verse, and 'he knows the ending and weeps anyway', with a near-identical fork and myth. Re-angled the hook, the first teach move, the fork, one myth item and the trapdoor onto the sisters' shared sentence (John 11:21 and 11:32, both quoted); Jesus wept stays, briefly, as the index requires. Cut the modern saying 'love with nowhere to go'.

Audit: John 11:37 has some of the mourners asking 'Could not this man... have caused that even this man should not have died?'; the teach and the myth reveal now say so instead of implying the whole crowd read the tears only as love.
